notes.meaning: The day arrived when Haman's order to destroy the Jews was set to be carried out. Their enemies hoped to overpower them, but God completely reversed the situation so that the Jews overcame those who hated them.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Few modern historians view the events of Esther as literal history, often questioning whether an empire-wide battle could have taken place without Persian records mentioning it.

notes.meaning: The Jews gathered together in their cities across the empire to defend themselves against anyone trying to harm them. No attacker could stand against them because great fear and dread fell on all the surrounding people. When God's people stand united, He gives them courage against their spiritual enemies.
The Persian governors, rulers, and officials chose to help the Jews instead of attacking them. They did this because they respected and feared Mordecai, who had gained high standing with the king.
Mordecai had become very powerful inside the royal palace. His reputation for wisdom and influence spread through all the provinces as he grew greater each day.
The Jews struck down their armed enemies with swords and defeated them completely. They were able to overcome all who had conspired to destroy them under Haman's original plot.
Within the fortress city of Susa, the Jews killed five hundred men who attacked them. These men belonged to the violent faction in the capital that remained determined to wipe out the Jews.
This list records the names of the ten sons of Haman, who had joined their father's wicked plot against God's people. All ten were killed in the fighting in Susa.

The Jews killed Haman's ten sons, but they did not take any of their property. Even though the king's law allowed them to take plunder, they took nothing to prove they were only defending their lives and not acting out of greed.
At the end of the day, officials reported the number of people killed in the citadel of Susa directly to the king. Xerxes received an exact count of the five hundred men who had fallen.

The king told Queen Esther about the five hundred men and Haman's ten sons killed in Susa, noting that far more must have fallen in the other provinces. He then asked what more she wanted, promising to grant whatever else she requested.

Esther asked the king to let the Jews in Susa defend themselves for one more day, and to hang the dead bodies of Haman's ten sons on the gallows. She wanted to finish breaking the power of this hostile group and make a public warning against attacking God's people.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some critical commentators view Esther's request as vengeful and bloodthirsty, arguing that an extra day of killing went beyond reasonable self-defense.

notes.meaning: The king approved Esther's request and issued another decree in Susa. The bodies of Haman's ten sons were then publicly hung on poles as a visible sign of their complete defeat.
On the fourteenth day of Adar, the Jews in Susa assembled again and put to death three hundred more of their enemies. Just as on the day before, they did not touch any plunder.

Across the rest of the Persian provinces, the Jews gathered to defend themselves and killed seventy-five thousand of their attackers. Even with such a massive victory, they refused to take any goods or wealth from the dead.
The fighting across the provinces took place on the thirteenth day of Adar. On the fourteenth day, the people rested from the conflict and made it a celebration of joy and feasting.
The Jews in Susa fought on both the thirteenth and fourteenth days, so they did not rest until the fifteenth day. That day became their special time of feasting and thanksgiving.

Because the Jews living in open country towns finished fighting in one day, they kept the fourteenth of Adar as their regular holiday. They celebrated with great joy, good food, and gifts of food shared with their neighbors.

Mordecai wrote an official account of these events and sent letters to all the Jews across the entire Persian Empire. He wanted every Jewish family, near and far, to understand how God had rescued them.

Mordecai told the people to celebrate both the fourteenth and fifteenth days of Adar every year. These were the days their sorrow turned to joy, so they were to feast, send food to friends, and give gifts to the poor.
The Jews agreed to make this celebration an ongoing custom, just as they had begun doing and as Mordecai had written. They accepted the responsibility to keep the festival alive for years to come.
Haman had plotted to wipe out the Jews and had cast the lot, called the Pur, to pick the day for their ruin. He trusted in superstitious lots, but God was always the one directing events.
When the plot was exposed to the king, he gave written orders that caused Haman's evil plan to fall back on his own head. As a result, Haman and his sons were executed on the gallows.

The people named this annual celebration Purim after the Persian word Pur, which means a lot. They established it because of the instructions in Mordecai's letter and because of the deliverance they had seen with their own eyes.
The Jews bound themselves, their descendants, and any who joined their faith to keep these two days every year without fail. They committed to following the written rules at the appointed time.
Purim was to be remembered and celebrated by every family, city, and province throughout all generations. The memory of God's great rescue was never to fade from their people.
Queen Esther and Mordecai wrote a second letter with full royal authority to confirm the rules of Purim. Their joint decree gave the festival the backing of official Persian law.
Mordecai sent these official letters to all the Jews across the 127 provinces of King Xerxes. His letters carried words of peace and truth, bringing comfort and certainty to the people.

These letters established the exact dates for Purim just as Esther and Mordecai had directed. They also included reminders of their previous times of fasting and crying out to God, so they would remember how He answered their desperate prayers.

Esther's royal decree confirmed all these instructions about Purim, and the account was written down in the historical records. God used her leadership to make sure this great rescue would never be forgotten.

other.label: Catholic and Orthodox
other.view: Catholic and Orthodox Bibles include additional Greek passages in Esther that expand the ending and add explicit prayers and mentions of God throughout the book.
